q: In the Orders schema, customer: Customer has no !. What does that tell a client?
options: The field may be null, for example when the customer lookup fails
The field is optional to select in a query, unlike non-null fields
The field is loaded lazily, only after the rest of the order
The field can be read but not set by a mutation
explain: Without ! a field is nullable, the default in GraphQL: the server may return null, for instance after an error, and the client must handle it. Every field is optional to select, nullable or not; the ! is a promise about the value, not about the query.

q: The schema says orders: [Order!]! and customer: Customer!. For one order out of three, the customer resolver throws. What does the client receive?
options: Three orders, the failed one with customer: null and an error
Two orders: the failed one is dropped from the list, with an error
"data": null and one entry in errors
An HTTP 500 response, with the error message in the body
explain: A non-null field cannot be null, so the error nulls its parent order; the order is non-null in the list, so the list goes; the list is non-null, so data becomes null (measured with graphql-js 16.14.2). A customer: null answer happens only when customer is nullable.

q: The live orders list uses a Relay-style connection. How does the back office ask for the next page?
options: It sends a page argument one higher than on the previous request
It sends pageInfo.endCursor back as after
It sends the id of the last node it received as an offset argument
It repeats the same query with first doubled each time
explain: A connection returns pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }, and the client passes endCursor as after to continue: the keyset pagination of M05 behind an opaque cursor. Page numbers and offsets are what cursors replace, because they repeat or skip rows when data changes.

q: Why does a resolver that loads "the customer of this order" send 21 queries for a page of 20 orders?
options: graphql-js turns each selected field into its own SQL join, one per order
Each call sees only its own parent order, so it loads one customer
The back office sent one GraphQL operation per order on the page
graphql-js retries every resolver once before returning its value
explain: graphql-js calls the customer resolver once per order, with that order as the parent, so the naive code sends one query per order plus one for the list: 21 measured with graphql-js 16.14.2. GraphQL does not generate joins; batching with DataLoader is the fix.

q: Why are DataLoaders created per request, in the context factory, rather than once at startup?
options: A DataLoader instance can run only one batch, then must be thrown away
Loaders created per request collect more keys in each of their batches
Its cache is per instance: shared, it would leak data across users and go stale
graphql-js refuses a context object that was already used by another request
explain: DataLoader memoises results per instance; its README recommends a new instance per request and warns that its cache does not replace Redis or Memcache. A process-wide loader would leak data between viewers and serve stale rows. Batching works the same either way.

q: Where does graphql.org recommend putting authorisation logic in production?
options: In the business layer every entry point calls, given a fully loaded user
In a schema directive on each type, evaluated by the GraphQL server alone
In an HTTP middleware placed in front of /graphql for every request
In the client, which should not request the fields it is not allowed to see
explain: graphql.org says to delegate authorisation to the business logic layer, the single source of truth shared by GraphQL, REST and jobs. It mentions directives as an option and says the logic should still stay in that layer. A middleware before /graphql cannot know which objects and fields the query will reach.

q: A request contains 100 aliases of order(id:) with different ids. With no limits configured, what does the server do?
options: Runs the resolver once, then copies the result into the 100 aliases
Rejects the operation during validation, as too many aliases are invalid
Runs the order resolver 100 times within the one request
Executes only the first alias and returns null for the 99 others
explain: Aliases are legal GraphQL, so each one is a separate field execution: measured with graphql-js, 100 aliases ran the resolver 100 times. A rate limiter counting requests sees one, which is why graphql.org recommends breadth and alias limits.

q: What makes trusted documents a real guardrail, when automatic persisted queries (APQ) are not?
options: Trusted documents are compressed, so they are cheaper to execute on the server
Only build-time operations run; APQ stores any query a client sends
Trusted documents also turn off introspection and field suggestions
APQ applies to mutations only, so queries remain unrestricted with it
explain: With trusted documents the server executes only known ids, so an arbitrary query never runs. APQ lets the client register any query after a PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND answer: it saves bandwidth, but any client can still run anything. Neither one turns off introspection.

q: The GraphQL server answers 200 for partial results. Which metric tells on-call that the order screen is failing?
options: The rate of 5xx responses returned by /graphql, per minute
The average response size of /graphql, compared with last week
The number of HTTP 4xx responses, grouped by client application
Errors per operation and per extensions.code, read from bodies
explain: Field errors arrive in the errors array next to partial data, usually with a 2xx status, so 5xx and 4xx rates stay flat while the screen breaks. Counting errors per operation and per code from the body is what shows it. Status codes only separate request errors (400, 422 in the draft spec) from executed ones.

q: Which change does graphql-js report as breaking?
options: Adding a field to Order
Changing an output field from String to String!
Adding an optional argument
Changing an output field from Int! to Int
explain: Loosening an output field to nullable breaks clients that relied on the non-null promise: findBreakingChanges reported FIELD_CHANGED_KIND (measured on 16.14.2). Tightening an output to non-null only strengthens the promise and was safe; an optional argument was "dangerous", not breaking.

q: Order status updates flow only from the server to the customer's browser. Which transport is the sensible default?
options: Server-sent events over HTTP/2
WebSockets with ws
Short polling every second
A GraphQL mutation called every few seconds
explain: SSE is built for one-way push over plain HTTP: cookies, load balancers and logs work unchanged, and EventSource reconnects with Last-Event-ID. WebSockets add a protocol, heartbeats and reconnection you do not need for one-way traffic, and polling every second would cost a request per client per second.

q: Why does the /live server send a ping to every socket every 30 seconds?
options: To measure the bandwidth of each client and adapt the message size
Because RFC 6455 requires a ping on every connection every 30 seconds
To find dead sockets and keep 60-second proxy idle timeouts from firing
To refresh the agent's session cookie before it expires on the server
explain: A socket with no pong since the last round is dead and is terminated, and the ping traffic keeps idle timeouts such as nginx's 60-second default from firing. RFC 6455 defines ping and pong but sets no interval; 30 seconds is the ws README's example.

q: The customer service times out for one order of the 50 shown on the live list. What do agents see, and what would you change?
code:
type Query { orders(first: Int!, after: String): [Order!]! }
type Order { id: ID! status: OrderStatus! customer: Customer! }
options: 49 complete orders and one with a null customer; nothing needs changing
An empty screen, as data is null; make customer nullable
All 50 orders, because GraphQL retries the failed resolver once more
An HTTP 504 from the GraphQL server, so the client shows its error page
explain: The error on the non-null customer nulls the order, which nulls the non-null list, which nulls data: one slow service blanks the whole screen (measured with graphql-js). A field that crosses to another service should be nullable; the "one null customer" outcome is exactly what that change buys.

q: What is wrong with this code, which does batch correctly?
options: Nothing: a loader shared across requests batches more keys, so it is faster
The loader must be created inside the resolver function, on every call
load must be awaited inside the resolver, or batching breaks
Its cache lives as long as the process: stale rows, shared across viewers
explain: DataLoader caches per instance, so a module-scope loader is a process-wide cache with no expiry and no per-user scope; the README recommends one instance per request. Creating it inside the resolver would break batching, since each call would get its own loader. Returning the promise without await is fine.

q: This batch function returns the rows as PostgreSQL gives them. Two of the requested ids were deleted. What goes wrong?
options: Values pair with keys by position, so a short array in any order breaks the contract
PostgreSQL rejects = ANY($1) when the parameter is a text array
DataLoader retries the two missing ids one by one, in a second batch
Nothing: DataLoader pairs each row with its key by reading the id field
explain: The DataLoader README requires an array of values of the same length as the keys, where each index corresponds to the same index in the keys. Rows come back in no guaranteed order and missing ids shorten the array. DataLoader never inspects an id field: map rows by id and return ids.map(...) with null for missing ones.

q: A page of 20 orders belongs to 5 distinct customers. With DataLoader's default options, how many keys does the batch function receive?
options: 20, one per order
5, one per distinct customer
1, because DataLoader loads one key per tick
25, the orders plus the customers
explain: With the cache enabled (the default), a key already requested in this loader is not sent again; its promise resolves from the same batch, per the README. Duplicates reach the batch function only with cache: false. Batching sends all distinct keys of the tick at once, not one.

q: A customer calls node(id: "T3JkZXI6OTk=") and receives another customer's order, although order(id:) checks ownership. What is the root cause?
options: Global ids are base64, so they are guessable; switching to UUIDs fixes it
The check lives in one resolver, not in the layer every path calls
node fields are unsafe by design and must be disabled in production
GraphQL cannot express authorisation per object, only per type
explain: The same Order is reachable from several fields; a check in order(id:) protects only that path. graphql.org recommends the business logic layer as the single source of truth. Unguessable ids reduce enumeration but are not authorisation, as M12's BOLA section says.

q: With the cost rule of section 4 (a field costs 1 per parent row; a list field multiplies its children by first), what does this operation cost?
explain: The outer orders costs 1, its 50 customer fields cost 50, the inner orders fields cost 50, and their id fields 50 × 50 = 2,500: 2,601, as measured. One more level multiplied it to 130,101, which is why each nested list needs to count.

q: The GraphQL endpoint is rate-limited to 100 requests per second per client, yet one client still takes replicas to 100% CPU. What do you add?
options: A lower request limit per client, such as 10 requests per second
Depth, alias and cost limits, and a budget charged per operation cost
More replicas behind the load balancer, with autoscaling on CPU
GET instead of POST, so the CDN absorbs most of the repeated load
explain: One GraphQL request can be arbitrarily expensive, so counting requests misses the problem; graphql.org recommends cost analysis and charging cost against a client budget. A lower request limit still lets one deep query through, and replicas only spread the same expensive work.

q: A colleague says: "We disabled introspection in production, so attackers cannot discover the schema." What do you answer?
options: Agreed: without introspection, nobody outside can discover the schema
Introspection must stay on, because every client needs it at run time
Agreed, and turning it off also blocks the alias and depth attacks
It is obscurity: "Did you mean" errors still leak field names
explain: graphql.org calls disabling introspection alone "security through obscurity". Measured with graphql-js, an unknown field produced "Cannot query field "total" on type "Order". Did you mean "note"?", which leaks names; GraphQL Armor can block field suggestions. Clients do not need introspection at run time; tooling does.

q: The prototype executes queries with graphql-js directly. A resolver throws the error below. What does the client receive?
options: A masked message, "Unexpected error.", with the real one in the logs
An HTTP 500 with an empty body, and the order screen shows nothing
order: null, and the raw message, IP included, in errors
Nothing visible: the field is silently null and errors stays empty
explain: graphql-js puts the thrown message in the error as is (measured), so database addresses leak. Masking to "Unexpected error." is what Yoga does by default; with Apollo Server you mask in formatError. Only a deliberately thrown GraphQLError should reach clients.

q: An agent tries to cancel an order that has already shipped. How should cancelOrder report it?
options: A union result with an OrderAlreadyShipped type and its shippedAt
A thrown GraphQLError, with the HTTP status set to 409 Conflict
null, and the screen tells the agent that something went wrong
CancelOrderSuccess, with a warning added under extensions
explain: An expected business outcome is data the client must act on, so it belongs in the schema as a typed result; generated client types then force the screen to handle it. A thrown error lands in an untyped errors array, and the HTTP status of a GraphQL response does not carry per-field outcomes.

q: The catalogue team wants product queries over GraphQL to be cached by the CDN. What works?
options: Add Cache-Control: public to the POST responses of /graphql
Configure the CDN to use the request body as part of its cache key
Expose the products through subscriptions instead of queries
Persisted query hashes over GET, with Cache-Control on the response
explain: HTTP caches key on method and URL, and every POST to /graphql looks the same. The spec allows GET for queries, and Apollo's docs pair hashed queries over GET with CDN caching, since full queries rarely fit in a cacheable URL. Subscriptions push events and are not cached.

q: You add REFUNDED to enum OrderStatus. Which statement is right?
options: It is safe: additive changes to a schema never affect existing clients
It is breaking: old clients fail validation when they meet the value
It is dangerous: old apps may get a value they do not handle
It is breaking: it changes the meaning of the existing enum values
explain: findDangerousChanges reported VALUE_ADDED_TO_ENUM (measured on graphql-js 16.14.2): old operations still validate, but a client switch with no default case may crash or show nothing. Mobile apps that stay installed for months make this the classic trap.

q: Socket.io runs on 6 pods behind a Kubernetes Service without session affinity. Clients keep failing to connect and fall back again and again. What is the likely cause?
options: Socket.io cannot run on more than one pod without its cluster adapter
The Redis adapter is missing, and Socket.io refuses connections without it
Kubernetes Services do not forward the WebSocket upgrade between pods
Long-polling requests of one session land on different pods: no stickiness
explain: Socket.io's docs say long-polling needs sticky sessions because a session spans several HTTP requests that must reach the server holding it; with only the WebSocket transport, one connection stays on one pod. The Redis adapter is about broadcasting across pods, not about connecting.

q: The back office uses SSE over HTTP/1.1. An agent opens order streams in seven tabs, and the seventh never loads. Why?
options: Over HTTP/1.1 a browser opens about 6 connections per domain; use HTTP/2
EventSource supports a single open stream per page and per tab
Node closes the oldest open response once six streams are open
The load balancer pins each agent to one pod, which refuses a seventh stream
explain: MDN documents the limit of 6 connections per browser and domain for SSE over HTTP/1.x; over HTTP/2 the number of streams is negotiated, 100 by default. Nothing in Node or EventSource limits streams per page.

q: The /live socket is authenticated by the session cookie. A pentester shows that a page on another site opens /live as the logged-in agent. What is the fix?
options: Pass the session token in the URL query string instead of the cookie
Check Origin against an allowlist at the upgrade; refuse with 403
Switch from ws:// to wss:// so the cookie is encrypted
Enable permessage-deflate and sign every message with a secret
explain: Browsers send cookies with the WebSocket handshake, so a hostile page can open a socket in the agent's name: Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking. OWASP says to validate Origin on every handshake with an allowlist, and RFC 6455 suggests 403 for a refused origin. Tokens in URLs leak into logs, and TLS does not stop a cross-site request.

q: With this send function, one agent's laptop sleeps with the tab open and the replica's memory climbs for hours. What is happening?
options: The client reads nothing, so messages queue in server memory: cap bufferedAmount
ws leaks memory whenever a socket stays open for more than a few hours
The heartbeat timer keeps references to sockets that are already closed
The operating system socket buffers grow without limit for a sleeping peer
explain: send() never blocks: what the peer does not read stays in the server's queue. Measured with ws 8.22.0, after about 2.5 MB went into OS buffers, bufferedAmount reached 10.4 MB for 200 messages of 64 KB and kept growing. The OS buffers are bounded; the process queue is not.

q: Replica 5 holds a customer's SSE stream. While replica 5 spends 2 seconds reconnecting to Redis, replica 2 publishes SHIPPED on the pub/sub channel. What happens?
options: Redis keeps the message until replica 5 subscribes to the channel again
Redis retries the delivery three times, then drops it with a warning
The browser notices, reconnects with Last-Event-ID and gets it
It is lost (at-most-once): resync from the database or use Redis Streams
explain: The Redis docs state that a pub/sub message a subscriber cannot handle, for example during a disconnect, is lost forever. The browser's stream to replica 5 never broke, so EventSource does not reconnect and nothing replays: the replica must resync itself, or read from a stream that keeps entries.

q: In the support chat, the customer's app resends a message after a timeout, but the first attempt had been stored. How do you make sure it is shown once?
options: Socket.io delivers exactly once, so the app should never resend at all
Deduplicate on the agent's screen by comparing the texts of messages
A client clientMessageId, a unique constraint and ON CONFLICT
Lock the conversation row until the client acknowledges the ack it got
explain: Resending until acked gives at-least-once delivery, and a client-generated id with a unique constraint turns it into once-only storage: the idempotency key of M05 applied to chat. Socket.io's default is at-most-once, per its docs, and two identical texts can be two real messages.
